title: LLM Performance Predictors: Learning When to Escalate in Hybrid Human-AI Moderation Systems
venue: Proc. of the 25th International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems (AAMAS 2026)
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of when to trust a large language model’s output versus when to escalate to a human reviewer in hybrid human-AI content moderation systems. The authors frame this as an uncertainty quantification and selective classification problem: a system should automate easy cases and defer risky ones to human review. They propose a new meta-model based on LLM Performance Predictors (LPPs) derived from model outputs, including token probabilities, entropy, verbalized confidence, and explicit uncertainty-attribution indicators.

The approach is evaluated on two moderation benchmarks: the OpenAI Moderation dataset and a multimodal moderation dataset spanning text, video, transcripts, thumbnails, and multiple languages. The experiments compare several proprietary and open-source LLMs and show that the proposed meta-model often improves error prediction and reduces expected moderation cost relative to baseline uncertainty heuristics such as maximum softmax probability, entropy, and top-2 margin. In some cases, however, performance is mixed under distribution shift, and the paper notes model-dependent limitations.

The paper is not a K–12 education study and does not involve teachers, students, classrooms, or instructional coaching. It is a technical systems paper about human-AI moderation workflows. Its main conclusion is that uncertainty-aware routing can improve operational efficiency and explainability in moderation, but the authors also note limitations such as the need for labeled data, the possibility of calibration issues, and mixed generalization across model families and datasets.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: A Google family of large language models used here as a base model for content-moderation classification and uncertainty estimation in a hybrid human-AI workflow.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as one of several LLMs whose outputs were used to predict correctness and decide whether to trust the model or escalate cases to human reviewers in content moderation tasks.

findings.finding_summary: Across the OpenAI Moderation dataset, Gemini-family models showed lower expected cost under the proposed meta-model than under baseline uncertainty heuristics. For example, gemini-2.5-flash-lite decreased from $122 to $77 expected cost with escalations falling from 315 to 227, and gemini-2.0-flash-lite decreased from $74 to $41 with escalations falling from 248 to 162.
findings.measure: Expected cost ($) and escalation count in selective escalation policy
findings.sample_size: n=1,680 texts (OpenAI Moderation); n=1,500 videos (Multimodal Moderation)

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical systems paper, but it is not a teacher-facing or K–12 instructional coaching study. The evidence is based on benchmark evaluations in content moderation rather than a controlled education intervention.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are operational and context-specific, showing cost reductions and fewer escalations in moderation workflows. There is no direct educational impact or teacher-use evidence, and no negative or null effect on K–12 coaching to assess.
